item.title: Amsterdam hopes 20km/h cycle lane limit will change behaviour
item.description:
Amsterdam hopes 20km/h cycle lane limit will change behaviour

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam city council has introduced an experimental speed limit of 20km/h for cyclists to see if riders can be persuaded to slow down.

Tourists, commuters and shoppers have all complained in recent years of feeling unsafe on the capital’s congested bike paths, but the only speed restriction is a 30 km/h limit for motor vehicles.

A temporary speed limit has been set on a section of Amstelveenseweg, one of the main routes into the city from the south, for four weeks to gauge its effect on cyclists’ behaviour.

But instead of enforcing the limit through fines and cautions, the city council has put up boards showing people how many of their fellow bike users are staying below 20 km/h, in the hope they will nudge people into being more considerate.

Traffic alderman Elise Moeskops told AT5 the idea of the experiment is to see if the signs will encourage a shift in cycling culture.

“If you enforce everything in the city you end up with a very harsh police state, and we don’t have the staff for that,” she said.

Infrastructure problems

“Are people prepared to cycle more slowly if we remind them that that’s an option? The question is what the social norm is on the cycle lane, because we don’t really know.”

But Kees Bakker, spokesman for the cyclists’ union Fietsersbond, was sceptical of the idea. He said better infrastructure was the solution to crowded bike lanes.

“The cycle lane on that road is very narrow and poorly laid out,” he told Dutch News. “There’s a busy pavement alongside it, so pedestrians spill over to the cycle path.

“It doesn’t make much difference if the speed limit is 20 km/h or 50 km/h, because the path is too narrow and there’s no room to overtake.”

Bakker said speed limits were likely to be less effective in bike lanes because not all cyclists travel at the same speed and they need space to overtake.

“Cars mostly drive in file at 30 km/h, but the range of speeds is much wider for cyclists,” he said. “Some of them ride at 15 km/h, others do 25 or even 30. There needs to be room to accommodate everyone, including people who want to coast along side by side at 15 km/h.”

item.title: Dutch destinations: Go back in time in eastern Drenthe
item.description:
Dutch destinations: Go back in time in eastern Drenthe

October 20, 2026 Robin Pascoe

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eastern Drenthe is perhaps the most underrated part of the Netherlands. Its rolling scenery, its history and its villages – low thatched farmhouses, tiny brick churches and woodlands – make it a perfect place to spend a few sunny autumn days.

Assen is the provincial capital. It has the region’s main museum and boasts the second-biggest department store in the Netherlands. It is also home to the Dutch TT circuit, offering a wide variety of motorcycle races from April to October. But the real charm of the region is in the countryside.

A weekend is not enough to take in everything, so here is a taster of what eastern Drenthe has to offer.

What to do

Visit the hunebedden
Eastern Drenthe is all about hunebedden, the Neolithic burial chambers built by the Funnel Beaker people over 5,000 years ago. Drenthe is home to 52 of the 54 known hunebedden in the Netherlands, and many are concentrated around Borger, where the national hunebed centre is based.

The biggest hunebed, with the not-so-romantic name D27, is located in the woods next to the visitors’ centre. The grounds are also home to a bizarre collection of zwerfstenen, or boulders, which were brought down to the province from Scandinavia by glaciers. Many of the stones have labels showing exactly where in Sweden or Norway they came from.

In addition, the centre has a café and a sort of Neolithic playground – the Prehistoric Park – where children can check out recreations of ancient homes. During peak season volunteers in costume are on hand to explain about the lives of people who lived in the region and demonstrate ancient crafts. No dogs.

Walk along the Hondsrug
The Hondsrug (literally “dog’s back”) is listed as a Unesco Global Geopark because of its unique history, deriving from the last two ice ages. This 70-kilometre-long glacial ridge made of sand and clay is the only one of its kind in Europe. There are dozens of walking and cycle trails to explore, as well as small museums, such as the De Nabershof working farm near Emmen. You can find out more about the region’s geology at the visitors centre, next to the hunebed centre in Borger.

Stroll around Orvelte
About 20 minutes south of Assen is Orvelte, a Drenthe village untouched by time, which has become a sort of open-air museum. It’s car-free – you park on the outskirts – but there is a horse-drawn “bus” if you have little ones with you who don’t want to walk.

Stroll past the thatched farmhouses, stop off for what we were told is the best apple pie in Drenthe, and check out the little museums – which seem to be based largely on the locals’ hobbies, such as collecting model cars and rare sheep.

There is a good sprinkling of shops, some of which sell tourist tat, but some are upmarket outlets selling wonderful antique pottery and glass, as well as clothes and bric-a-brac. Plenty of options for lunch and morning coffee. If you are into Christmas themes, Orvelte will transform into a Christmas village from December 18 to 20.

Catch up on history at the Drents Museum in Assen
The Drents Museum in the provincial capital Assen hit the headlines in 2025 when criminals broke in overnight and stole a number of priceless gold relics, most of which have since been recovered. There is no Romanian gold on show any longer – the current special exhibition is about Angkor in Cambodia – but the museum is well worth a visit to find out more about the history of the region.

It is heavy on the infotainment, so there’s plenty to keep the kids occupied, but the museum nevertheless has something for everyone. Located in several buildings linked by tunnels and overground walkways, the museum has Neolithic finds, art (a couple of Van Goghs), recreated stijlkamers (period rooms), temporary exhibitions and a fine café for lunch.

Go on a tree walk
The Boomkroonpad – treetop path – takes you from the roots of an oak tree up into the treetops, where you can walk along a very solid metal structure and admire the forest from above. The path is also the starting point for five forest floor walks, ranging from three to 16.5 kilometres, and there are plenty of organised activities for families – deer and mushroom spotting, for example – all year round.

Where to eat
All the attractions we visited had cafés for lunch, mainly selling standard-fare sandwiches and broodjes kroket. Assen has a good selection of cafés and restaurants for dinner. We ate at our hotel, Rikus, which uses local produce and offers three-, four- and five-course menus. Be warned: the portions are big as well as being delicious.

Where to stay
Rikus, a small hotel in the village of Eext, about 20 minutes from Assen and Borger, has an eclectic interior and big bedrooms with views over the countryside. As a couple we paid €331 for bed, breakfast, a three-course dinner and drinks.

There is a hotel and a quaint-looking B&B in Orvelte, and Assen is home to Hotel de Jonge, with a large café terrace in the heart of the old city. Drenthe is popular with Dutch holidaymakers, so, as you would expect, there are plenty of campsites and holiday parks to choose from as well.

Anything else
Unless you are big on cycling or long walks, you really need a car to get around the region. The attractions can get very busy at weekends in the summer months, which may well dent their charm. The Dutch TT Grand Prix takes place on the last Sunday in June.

item.title: Primary school teachers reject four-day week amid staff shortage
item.description:
Primary school teachers reject four-day week amid staff shortage

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

School leaders in the Netherlands are opting against the idea of a four-day week for primary schools amid a critical shortage of teachers.

A survey conducted by Nu.nl and the Academy & Association of School Leaders (AVS) found that of 308 heads of schools, only three (less than 1%) said they had chosen to reduce required attendance days for pupils as a solution to the crisis.

Primary schools are short of roughly 5,800 teachers nationwide, about 6.3% of all teachers, according to research institute Centerdata.

Despite an increase in teacher numbers since 2024, when the shortage stood at 8.1%, low salaries and long hours remain a problem for enticing people to join the profession. The previous generation of teachers is also retiring, worsening the gap.

Leanne der Steeg, a policy advisor at AVS, told Nu.nl that a four-day school week does not necessarily help the teachers and can harm education.

“A four-day school week also brings ‘hassle’ with it,” she said. “It is not just a matter of sending a class home. Thought must be given to the missed teaching time. Will it be made up at another time, will homework be assigned, and what about children of working parents? And if you free up a teacher for a day by opting for a four-day school week, it requires preparation before they can stand in front of another class.”

item.title: Rail fares to go up by 4.7% next year to help pay for new trains
item.description:
Rail fares to go up by 4.7% next year to help pay for new trains

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch national train operator NS is set to raise fares by almost 5% on average in 2027, exceeding the rate of inflation for the third year in a row.

The increases are needed “to purchase new, comfortable trains, pay for rising costs and keep investing in good services,” Daan Schut, the management board member responsible for fares, said in a press statement on Tuesday.

NS is offsetting the increase by offering bigger discounts on off-peak fares for passengers who buy in advance. The maximum reduction on so-called PrijsTijd deals will go up from 60% to 80% next year.

The company said it also wanted to discuss reviving the discounted summer subscription rate, which allowed passengers to travel off-peak and at weekends for €49 a month in July and August, rather than the regular fee of €127.50.

The Railrunner fare for children, which allows under-12s to travel across the country all day for a flat rate, is being frozen at €2.50, and the KidsVrij subscription for families, which gives free travel up to the age of 11, will stay unchanged.

The minimum fare for short journeys is going up to €3.10, while the supplement for the high-speed line between Schiphol and Rotterdam is rising by 20 cents to €3.40.

Rail passengers’ organisation Rover criticised the above-inflation rises, pointing to the success of the summer discount as proof that people will travel by train if it is an affordable option.

“Now that NS is finally seeing its passenger numbers growing, passengers are being punished with big ticket increases. By constantly using the maximum room that NS has to raise ticket prices, it is holding back further growth,” a Rover spokesperson said.

Fares have gone up by around 6.5% for each of the last two years, partly to correct the 1.5% rise in 2023, when inflation was 10%. In 2024 prices were frozen thanks to a government cash injection of €120 million.

NS made a profit for the first time in years in 2025, recording a net gain of €380 million, though most of this came from a recalculation of its access charges during the coronavirus pandemic, when fewer trains ran. The charges are the costs the company pays to use the track network.

item.title: Millions to get compensation from takeaway apps over hidden fees
item.description:
Millions to get compensation from takeaway apps over hidden fees

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Food delivery apps Thuisbezorgd and Uber Eats have been forced to stop hiding fees and advertising fake discounts after a complaint by consumer watchdog Consumentenbond.

Millions of customers will also receive a payout voucher in compensation ranging between €5 to €30, the watchdog said.

The companies were putting “small order fees” and other surcharges only at the end of orders, and were advertising misleading discounts for some takeaways.

The Consumentenbond accused Thuisbezorgd in July of hiding charges that often added €2 to €4 to an order. Fake discounts were also show; in one example, Indian snacks priced at €3.75 were later shown as “reduced” from €7.50 to €6.

Both companies told news agency ANP the changes followed “constructive” talks with the Consumentenbond. Uber Eats had already adjusted its charges in June.

item.title: Children of welfare households more likely to face unemployment
item.description:
Children of welfare households more likely to face unemployment

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Young adults who spent their teenage years in a household relying on benefits are far less likely to have a job by the age of 29, according to research by national statistics office CBS.

Some 69% of that group had a job at 29, compared with 89% of those whose families never claimed bijstand, the basic benefit for people with no other means of support.

The gap appears even after short periods on welfare. Of those whose household claimed for less than a year, 77% were working at 29 and 16% were living on benefits.

The same research shows education follows the same pattern. Around 20% of those who grew up partly on welfare had an hbo college or university degree by 29, against 50% of other young adults, and the number of years spent on welfare made little difference.

Those who do work earn less per hour, work fewer hours and are less likely to have a permanent contract: around 60% do, compared with 71% of employees who did not grow up on welfare.

The CBS followed 186,000 people who turned 18 in 2013 and lived in the Netherlands from age 12 to 18. One in 10 grew up at least partly in a household on welfare, and 3% for five years or more.

item.title: Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack
item.description:
Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, filed a police report on Monday over the cyberattack that forced it to take systems offline more than a week ago.

The company said in a statement on Monday that its investigation had confirmed the suspicious activity in its IT systems was caused by “the malicious actions of others”. Until now it had described the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”.

Police and the public prosecution service (OM) urged the company to file a report last week, because a criminal investigation cannot start without one.

It is not clear why Ahold Delhaize has now decided to do so, broadcaster NOS reported.

The company did notify the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the justice ministry’s cybersecurity agency, within 24 hours of discovering the attack, as required under a new cybersecurity law that came into force on August 15.

Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online and home deliveries are expected to resume on Friday, October 23, the company said. The websites of drugstore chain Etos and drinks chain Gall & Gall, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, are available again.

Ahold Delhaize said it had so far found no evidence that sensitive data belonging to customers, staff or business partners had been taken. It declined to give further details while the investigation continues, saying they could compromise its security.

The Albert Heijn hack is one of the first major incidents since the new reporting law came into force. It covers some 8,000 organisations seen as vital to the country, from healthcare, drinking water and banks to the food sector, including supermarkets.

The problems began on Sunday, October 11, when Albert Heijn switched off part of its IT systems, halting home deliveries and work at its distribution centres and leaving empty shelves in some stores.

Security sources told NOS last week that servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey had been used in the attack. Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad that the outage was costing the company “tens of millions” of euros a day.

item.title: POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation
item.description:
POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation

October 19, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Campaigners for the widows of former Japanese prisoners of war have said they will keep fighting for compensation after the Dutch government said only surviving partners would be entitled to receive their spouses’ unpaid wages.

Long-term care minister Mirjam Sterk announced last Friday that the partners of civil servants and servicemen who were held captive following the invasion of Indonesia in 1942 would receive 42 months’ back pay, covering the period until the liberation in May 1945.

But Sterk said only widows who are still alive when the compensation scheme is launched on February 1 next year, all of whom are well into their nineties or older, would receive the payouts because a more extensive ruling would be “too complicated”.

The government has also cut the total size of the fund from the €50 mln announced in its last spring budget statement to €11.5 mln, on the basis that only a few hundred widows of the 40,000 men who were captured by the Japanese still survive.

The decision follows decades of campaigning for victims of the camps to be given the same treatment as Dutch government employees who were forced to work in Germany during World War II.

Moluccans

They include Moluccans who later fought on the side of the Dutch during the Indonesian liberation war and were subsequently persecuted by the independent government, prompting them to flee to the Netherlands.

Earlier this year prime minister Rob Jetten apologised to the Moluccan community for the way they were treated when they arrived in the 1950s.

Peggy Stein, of campaign group Indisch Platform 2.0, called for the ruling to be backdated to include widows who were alive when parliament approved a motion by farmers’ party leader Caroline van der Plas on the issue last April.

“That was when these people heard they were going to get their wages, but some of them have died in the meantime,” she told Dutch News.

Stein added that the cabinet appeared to have pushed through the ruling without waiting for parliament to debate the extent of the compensation scheme first.

“We still had to talk to MPs and had asked for a committee debate, but never had a reply,” she said.

“This isn’t about care or morality, it’s purely and solely about the technical settling of a case for the lowest possible cost.”

No official records

Sterk said it was “practically impossible” to compensate relatives of former camp inmates who had died because the government had no central records, but Stein said her campaign group had compiled its own list of detainees and could provide documentation showing they worked for the colonial administration.

“I have a list, but they say the SVB [Dutch social security bank] is legally not allowed to use it,” she said. “But if they have €50 million to spend, why can’t they find other parties to distribute the money who are able to work with us?”

Stein said she was not calling for the regulation to be scrapped, but it should be backdated to 2025 or 2015, when the government first acknowledged that the POWs were in its service. Prior to that it had argued that the colonial government in Indonesia was a separate entity.

Stein said the campaigners would continue to press the cabinet to compensate all victims of the Japanese occupation, including those who were no longer alive. “We have made a promise to these elderly people, we have signed a petition, and we are going to keep fighting for it,” she said.

item.title: Body of missing woman from Amsterdam found in suitcase
item.description:
Body of missing woman from Amsterdam found in suitcase

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The body of a woman who went missing after taking a lift on a bike with an unknown man has been found in a suitcase in Amsterdam.

Police said the remains were discovered last Friday in the Amstel river and identified as a woman named as Hajar, who was last seen two weeks ago near the Rai conference centre.

She left in the direction of Buitenveldert on October 4 on a black ladies’ bike with a man whom police are now trying to trace.

Police would not confirm reports on AT5 that a passer-by found the suitcase containing the body on Saturday morning, or that messages were sent to local neighbourhood app groups later that day asking if people had noticed anybody acting suspiciously with a suitcase.

She is described as between 1.65m and 1.70m tall with dark curly hair and dark eyes. The day before she was last seen alive she was wearing a tiger print dress and white New Balance shoes.

Anyone who saw Hajar between October 4 and October 17 or has any information can contact police on 0900 8844, via www.politie.nl, or anonymously via 0800 7000 or at Meld Misdaad Anoniem.

item.title: How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data
item.description:
Partner content

How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data

October 19, 2026

A letter from the Belastingdienst has landed on the doormat, and it might as well be written in code. At work, the team meeting that began in English has drifted into Dutch, and you’re nodding along while hoping nobody asks for your opinion. Sound familiar? We spoke with OmniForge, a tech company helping expats tackle the language barrier online.

Why the usual AI tools fall short
AI assistants promise to help with both of these challenges, but they have their limits. Firstly, many recording and transcription tools only support a handful of major languages, which leaves plenty of expats working in English by default, says Daniel G. Ríos, co-founder and CEO of OmniForge. Secondly, most of them process everything in the cloud, which is less than ideal when it comes to an employment contract, payslip or document with your BSN on it.

The risk is not theoretical. When hackers posted Odido’s customer data online, millions of people were reminded how far personal data can travel. “In the best case scenario, your data might be used to profile you for ads,” Daniel says, “but in the case of data exfiltration from cloud providers, your data might also be used for nefarious purposes.”

A local alternative, built by expats
OmniForge is a privacy-first AI desktop app for macOS and Windows that transcribes meetings and answers questions about your documents, all on your own computer. It was built by a team of expats in the Netherlands who, as Daniel puts it, “experience the exact same bilingual friction our users do.”
https://omniforge.online/dutchnews

“People should not have to compromise on their personal information in order to benefit from a service,” he says. In practice, the AI engine lives on your machine rather than in a data centre. “You could disconnect your WiFi entirely, and it will still securely transcribe your meetings and analyse your documents.” Only account login and subscription management are online.

There’s an environmental upside too, Daniel argues: running AI on your own computer’s spare processing power, what he calls “Green AI at the Edge,” can avoid the electricity and cooling water that big cloud models require from data centres.

When the meeting switches language
Language is where OmniForge stands out. It transcribes audio in 25 languages, including Dutch, English, German, French, Spanish and Polish, and can write summaries and answers in around 200 languages. In other words, a meeting held in Dutch can be summarised in whichever language you read most comfortably.

Then there’s the meeting that starts in English and slides into Dutch. Other tools make you pick a language in advance, Daniel says, whereas OmniForge listens for mid-sentence switches. He admits the transcript does not always get the spoken language right, but because the summary can be generated in any supported language regardless of the input, the gist still comes through.

A typical user, he says, is an international professional in a technical project meeting where half the team defaults to Dutch. Instead of stopping the flow to ask for translations, they record locally, having the assurance that a full English summary will be waiting the moment the meeting ends.

Decoding the paperwork
The same tool works on documents, not just audio. You can drop a Dutch PDF into OmniForge, whether it’s a letter from your landlord or your VvE, a payslip or a notice from the Belastingdienst, then ask questions and get an explanation in English.

Phone calls are covered, too. If you’re talking to the gemeente, put the phone on speaker and record the conversation: even if you feel lost during the call, OmniForge transcribes it so you have a comprehensive summary to review the moment you hang up. “It takes the stress out of local administration,” is how Daniel puts it.

Built for international teams
For employers, the same features make onboarding and internal meetings more inclusive: colleagues who are not fully fluent can follow along through a summary in their preferred language. And because OmniForge records locally, there’s no bot joining your video calls. A project manager juggling several projects can also keep a workspace for each, store meetings and documents together, and ask the assistant for recaps or highlights.

Moreover, local processing represents a win for compliance: HR handles sensitive employee data, and client confidentiality is non-negotiable. Companies are increasingly wary of staff feeding sensitive information to AI chatbots, Daniel explains. “Keeping everything in-house means GDPR compliance by default.” Many cloud tools go to great lengths to get certified, he notes, “but that just means they took steps to secure their customers’ data. With OmniForge, each customer is the sole owner of their data.”

Limitations and next steps
Daniel is upfront about OmniForge’s limits. Because everything runs on your device, transcription speed depends on your hardware: a brand-new machine will get through an hour-long meeting much faster than an older laptop. The assistant is above-average at summaries, highlights and finding information in your documents, “but it cannot compete with the likes of ChatGPT or Claude in terms of raw intelligence,” Daniel concedes, since it has a fraction of the resources.

OmniForge’s next steps will focus on speeding up the models on older hardware and adding more regional dialects. A mobile version is also planned, depending on how many people adopt the app.

Try it on your next confusing letter
The best first step, Daniel says, is to try OmniForge on your next meeting or baffling Dutch letter. Paid tiers start at €9.99 per month for unlimited quotas for individual users. But there’s a generous free tier so you can try before you buy: 40 complimentary minutes per recording and 50 indexed files. All you need to do is download OmniForge for Mac or Windows for free and register.
